item.title: What Does It Mean to Believe in God?
item.description:
Religion

What Does It Mean to Believe in God?

Far from being blind, faith may entail the deepest insights.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • The human cognitive apparatus may operate with limits when it comes to believing in or 'knowing' God.
  • Math, logic, and science may not be the best paths by which to pursue such knowledge.
  • Other approaches, such as narrative, may be better suited to this challenge.

In his Ethics, Aristotle says that we should seek to understand each thing according to the kind of account it permits. In solving an arithmetic problem, for example, we should expect an answer that is both accurate and precise. In the moral life, by contrast, we should seek an account that accords with what a practically wise person would have to say.

If we are adding or subtracting single-digit numbers, we can reasonably expect a reliable answer from a third grader. If, however, we are talking about friendship, marriage, or the relationship between a parent and offspring, we should turn elsewhere for insight, perhaps to the works of George Eliot or Leo Tolstoy.

Burning Bush, 1850
Source: Logo of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland/public domain

A similar shift in expectation is appropriate when we think about belief in God. If God were a phenomenon susceptible to the sort of reasoning that we find in an arithmetic problem or a proof in symbolic logic, then it should be relatively easy to construct a knock-down argument for the existence and nature of God.

If, however, God is not quantifiable, then arithmetical approaches are not likely to serve us well, and if God is not like the major or minor premises of a syllogism (such as: All things we can conceive of exist; we can conceive of God; therefore, God exists), then we should not expect to “solve” God like a proof.

Likewise, if God is not made of matter, we should not expect to be able to reproduce the divine presence through scientific means, whether physical or chemical. The mere fact that God does not have mass, dimension, shape, location, or color does not establish that God is nothing more than a figment of human imagination.

After all, we believe in numbers, although they lack all the physical properties just mentioned, and we also believe in love, justice, beauty, and truth, although they too cannot be counted, logically proved, or reproduced in a laboratory flask. There are things we believe to be real that we cannot see with our eyes or touch with our hands.

If sacred texts are any guide, the best means we have of accounting for God are not the methods of mathematics, logic, or science, but those more closely aligned with literature or narrative. The Bible, for example, is full of stories, and while a few of these stories include God directly, many more address the effects of God’s presence in the unfolding of the human story.

In one well-known metaphor, God is not something we directly apprehend, but we can sense God at work in the world much as we see and hear the breeze rustling the leaves on a tree. When Moses first senses God’s presence, it is in the form of a bush that is burning but not consumed by the flames, something only he has the curiosity and patience to see.

At this point, a skeptic might ask, If God is real, is it too much to ask that the divine should simply appear before us, work a few miracles, and thereby remove all doubt? But what if the problem is not God’s but ours? What if God cannot be put into any humanly constructed box because the divine is far beyond our meager intellectual and imaginative capacities?

What if we are talking about a reality that undergirds all of reality, not only as we know it but also far beyond our capacity to comprehend? What if we are seeking not just a clockmaker who set things in motion billions of years ago but a creator who sustains the universe from moment to moment as it continues to unfold even now in space and time?

Even the physical universe is far beyond our capacity to keep tabs on. A mature human organism consists of about 40 trillion cells, each one of which performs about 1 billion chemical reactions per second, which in turn requires the presence of about 100 trillion atoms of hydrogen. Of course, these are just round numbers – only God knows for sure.

It is quite possible, perhaps likely, and based on past experience, all but certain that there is a great deal that we do not yet know about even the physical universe. It was only in 1895 that we first learned of the existence of x-rays and only in 1962 that we verified extra-terrestrial x-ray sources. What else still awaits our discovery?

Yet even to say that we still have a great deal more to discover hardly captures the full extent of the problem. For one thing, there may be more out there and in here, even if it is susceptible to our awareness or understanding, than we will ever uncover. And it is also possible that the greater part of it does not conform to our ways of knowing.

Perhaps being itself, as well as its source and end, is not an entirely anthropomorphic thing, in the sense that it is not built for our minds. It may have many other purposes far beyond us. And yet, here we are, blessed with the ability to perceive and understand some truly remarkable things, even if we can’t begin to get our hands around the whole thing.

Perhaps when it comes to God, poetry, music, art, and narrative are the best we can hope for – intimations, always allusive and never definitive. And yet, even here, we find truth and beauty for which we have every reason to be deeply thankful, for perhaps it is above all when we sense God’s presence, maybe with the aid of Eliot and Tolstoy, that we come most fully to life.

item.title: Beyond Us Versus Them
item.description:
Politics

Beyond Us Versus Them

On making our circles bigger.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • The ability to categorize is a natural and automatic function of the human brain.
  • When we form categories for groups of people, we can easily make false assumptions about someone.
  • One way to move past the “us versus them” mentality may be to find something you have in common.

On election day this month, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, stripping Republicans of a supermajority. Headlines surrounding the midterms focused on the rising tension between Democrats and Republicans amid the Trump administration, which has created a lot of rifts between neighbors, friends, and even family members across the country. After winning his race, Democratic U.S. Senator-Elect James Talarico of Texas pleaded with Americans to reframe the narrative, not as a "left versus right" ideological struggle, but as a "top versus bottom" economic divide between wealthy elites and working-class people.

Whether or not you’re a fan of Talarico, he might be on to something. The idea of “us versus them” is as old as the human race, and likely comes from our propensity to form categories. The ability to categorize is a natural and automatic part of the human brain; it allows us to store an incredible amount of information in our memories and make inferences about things we’ve never seen before. Imagine for a second that we didn’t have the ability to form categories; it would mean that every time we encountered a brand-new object, we’d have to learn about it from scratch. The fact that we have categories means that whenever we encounter an apple, for example, we can apply what we know about other apples and safely assume that this new apple is a piece of fruit that tastes sweet and is nutritious. Likewise, whenever we encounter a new dog, we’d know something about the way it likely behaves, what it eats, and whether it’s safe to approach.

Source: rawpixel / pxhere

Our propensity to categorize starts very early in our lives. By 2 months of age, infants can distinguish broad categories of animate versus inanimate objects. By 3 to 4 months, infants can make basic-level categories for things like cats, dogs, and birds, and by 6 to 7 months they can even form subordinate categories distinguishing among different types of dogs (e.g., Beagles versus St. Bernards). By 14 to 18 months, they can use an object’s function to form categories (even in the absence of physical similarity), and they begin to use labels to organize categories. Needless to say, categorization develops quite early in our lives and over time becomes automatic.

How Categorizing People Can Lead to Prejudice and Ingroup Bias

But despite its benefits, our natural propensity to categorize has some downsides when we extend the ability beyond the categorization of objects to the categorization of people. When we form categories for groups of people, we can easily make false assumptions about someone new purely based on their category membership. This behavior is the very definition of “prejudice,” which is the tendency to make assumptions about someone purely based on their membership in a particular group. On top of that, when people tend to place themselves in a group, or what we might call an “ingroup,” there will inevitably be others who are left out of that group—people we call “outgroup” members. Infants begin to do this based on perceptual features like gender and race by 6 months, and slightly older children expect that people in the same group—usually marked in research by sharing some arbitrary feature, like a shirt color—should like the same things and behave in similar ways (e.g., Liberman, Woodward, & Kinzler, 2017).

Why is this important? Not surprisingly, we treat people better when we think they’re part of our ingroup, even if that ingroup is completely arbitrary. For example, in a recent set of studies, researchers put adults in groups based on an arbitrary similarity (e.g., people who like green versus blue, or people who prefer squares versus triangles), along with more meaningful ones (e.g., political orientation, religious affiliation, ethnicity), and then had them play a game that required cooperation. The researchers found that the more group memberships people shared—regardless of whether they were meaningful groups or were completely arbitrary—the more people cooperated with each other (Uğurlar et al., 2024). And the fact that we cooperate more with group members who share commonalities with us that are completely trivial suggests that membership isn't necessarily fixed.

And in fact, the boundaries between “us” and “them” can shift depending on which aspects of our identities we emphasize. I've experienced this firsthand. I was only a 21-year-old college student on September 11, 2001, when the planes hit the World Trade Center in New York. Despite it being the scariest day of my life, I remember hundreds of students gathering on the quad, arms around each other’s shoulders, swaying and singing America the Beautiful. I never felt togetherness like that before, and I’m not sure if I’ve ever felt it since. During that tragedy, we weren’t Democrats and Republicans; we were all Americans. We were forced to reframe the ingroup that day—instead of being in separate smaller circles, we made the circle wider.

In real-life research testing this observation, researchers conducted a series of studies where they made participants’ American identity more salient (e.g., by writing a paragraph on why they are proud to identify as American). At the end of the exercise, both Democrat and Republican participants evaluated members of the opposing party more positively (Levendusky, 2018).

Moving Beyond “Us Versus Them” by Finding Common Ground

So perhaps one way to move past the “us versus them” mentality in politics, or in life more broadly, is to stop thinking about people as Republicans versus Democrats and instead, to find something you have in common—maybe you are fellow parents, fellow community members, fellow music lovers, or just fellow humans. As Talarico alluded to, by reframing our ideas of group membership—by defining our groups more broadly instead of narrowly—people who might otherwise seem different can now become members of a shared community.

item.title: Why Leaving an Abusive Partner May Not End the Pain
item.description:
Narcissism

Why Leaving an Abusive Partner May Not End the Pain

Grandiose narcissism predicts PTSD in their ex-partners.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Narcissism and psychopathy share common traits that cause interpersonal aggression.
  • In a 1,294-person study, partner grandiose narcissism predicted PTSD more strongly than abuse frequency.
  • Confidence alone is not a red flag of narcissism; emotional manipulation is also a factor.
Source: Image by pixel2013 from Pixabay

Many people have left an abusive relationship feeling heartbroken and relieved at the same time. Whether the abuse was emotional, physical, or both, many victims experience a temporary sense of relief, realizing their mental health is no longer linked to a partner’s toxic behavior. Or is it? Because recognizing symptoms helps identify appropriate treatment, it is helpful to understand the potential fallout from a maladaptive relationship, even after the fact.


Dark Triad Traits and PTSD

Shahida Arabi (2023) investigated the impact of partner narcissism and psychopathy on posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptomology. She explains that both dark triad traits share numerous common traits that may cause aggression within intimate partnerships, including grandiosity, manipulation, lack of empathy, and exploitation. Such personalities also engage in manipulative behavior, designed to keep partners insecure and emotionally unsteady. They shower romantic prospects with excessive attention and flattery commonly referred to as “love bombing,” shut down conversations or "stonewall," and “gaslight” partners by questioning their memory, reality, or perception.

Describing the characteristics of two narcissism subtypes, Arabi explains that grandiose narcissism is linked with higher amounts of self-esteem and self-confidence, while vulnerable narcissism is associated with fearfulness and hypersensitivity. Regarding the potential for victimization through aggression, Arabi recognizes the strong association between narcissistic and antisocial personality traits and perpetrating intimate partner violence, and the impact of intimate partner violence on the victim, including mental health problems and PTSD.

Grandiose Narcissism as the Greatest Problem

Of the dark personality traits, one type of narcissism may be uniquely damaging over time. Studying 1,294 subjects romantically involved with individuals expressing a high degree of narcissistic or psychopathic traits, Arabi found that grandiose and vulnerable narcissism were significant predictors of PTSD symptomology for ex-partners who had exited the relationship, even after factoring in the impact of previous abuse and manipulation.

Arabi found that grandiose narcissism expressed by a partner was the strongest predictor of PTSD, more so than frequency of abuse, childhood abuse, or physical abuse. It was also a stronger predictor than vulnerable narcissism or psychopathy, which Arabi opines may be due to the fact that grandiose narcissism is linked with a higher degree of self-aggrandizement, which could produce elevated self-blame and intrusive thoughts in victims who are abused by a more confident and ruthless person who has such traits.

Planning an Exit Sooner Rather Than Later

Considering the frequency with which we learn about and discuss the potential impact of dark personalities on romantic relationships, the goal is to ferret out such characteristics sooner rather than later. And although we gain more information as we spend time with someone over time, many people detect cues as early as a first date.

Detecting grandiose narcissism involves more than recognizing elevated self-esteem and self-confidence, which are not inherently negative characteristics on their own. Instead, look past the confident veneer to the cunning, venomous behaviors emerging over time as dark personalities begin to reveal their true colors.

Be attentive to subtle tactics of emotional manipulation, consider whether flattery is authentic and appropriate, and recognize that healthy romantic attention makes you feel desirable, but also valuable, cared for, and comfortable. Getting to know a potential paramour at a pace that is slow and steady affords time to decide if your new love interest genuinely possesses the traits of a good partner and will be a good fit for you.

item.title: The Harmful Consequences of a Frictionless Life
item.description:
Relationships

The Harmful Consequences of a Frictionless Life

Why friction is necessary for healthy human relationships.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • We need to experience friction in relationships to learn how to survive.
  • The development of emotional intelligence requires us to be vulnerable, take risks, hurt and be hurt.
  • The development of social intelligence requires experiences of getting things wrong and being wronged.
Friction is necessary for human development and growth
Source: Free download: Pixabay/ thommas68

I recently wrote a post titled, “The Impact of AI on Who We Are and Who We Become”. In it, I stated that development of the “self” relies heavily on friction, trial-and-error and navigating the unknown. I asserted that by replacing these struggles with optimised, predictable convenience, AI threatens active self-discovery and perhaps even challenges the very concept of “self”. The concept of a frictionless life is one I’ve continued to contemplate. We need friction. It invites us to examine our biases and assumptions. It helps us to develop and grow.

The counterpart to friction is perhaps perfection, a theme I discussed in a more recent post. The promise of perfect communication is one of the allures of AI companionship. People turn to chatbots in an effort to avoid the messy, imperfect realties of human relationships. But guess what? A frictionless life is a fantasy, and so, when friction does inevitably show up in human relationships, people then can’t handle it. They panic. They employ psychological defences. They attack. I see this play out on social media, where the algorithm traps us in silos where everyone agrees with us. I don’t think we learn much in silos. There’s no friction. There’s no space to explore biases and assumptions. There’s no room to grow. I’ve also seen what happens when an adversary slides in from left field: Fear. Ragebait. Cancellation.

I often hear the phrase, “I don’t like conflict,” and who does? But what that phrase often means is, “I don’t know how to manage it; I haven’t got the skills.” In psychoanalytic literature there’s a concept called “rupture and repair”,1 which describes what happens when there is a split or lack of attunement (the rupture) followed by a renewed closeness and connection (the repair). This comes from psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott’s observations of what he termed “good-enough” mothering, where ruptures are inevitable, though hopefully occasional. During infancy, the baby uses opportunities of misattunement to learn to tolerate frustration, regulate their emotions and develop a sense of self. They learn to manage friction. A rupture in any relationship, including therapeutic ones, presents an opportunity. It is often the struggle moments, if we can survive them, that facilitate connectedness and change.

But what if we cannot survive them? What if we never learned or have forgotten how? Whereas a lack of “good-enough” early experiences deny infants the opportunity to develop the skills necessary for reparation, AI chatbots generate a kind of unlearning which leads to unrealistic expectations about the complexities of human relationships. This can lead to social atrophy and a lack of conflict resolution skills. It can lead to emotional detachment and withdrawal. It can fuel fear and rage.

Human connections are messy, imperfect, unpredictable and clumsy. We “um” and we “er”. We say the wrong thing. We misunderstand and are misunderstood. We make mistakes. We are vulnerable. We might cause offence or be offended. We might cause or be hurt. These are the struggle moments that AI chatbots eradicate. Artificial companions never misunderstand. They are always validating and affirming, infinitely agreeable and sycophantic. They never get frustrated or impatient. They don’t misunderstand us or tell us we’ve made a mistake. They are not vulnerable and they can’t get hurt or offended. Our interactions with chatbots are always frictionless and they carry zero risk. They teach us nothing, however, about what it’s like to be in relationship with an imperfect human.

The development of emotional intelligence requires us to be vulnerable, take risks, hurt, be hurt and survive. The development of social intelligence requires friction – experiences of getting things wrong and being wronged and surviving. Struggle moments present valuable opportunities to deepen relationships. A frictionless life is a fantasy. Opting out of messy human relationships and choosing to live in that fantasy helps no one.

item.title: "Born to Be Wild": How Zoos Fail to Protect Their Residents
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

"Born to Be Wild": How Zoos Fail to Protect Their Residents

Andrew Westoll explains why high-quality lives are not happening at the zoo.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • The new book "Born to Be Wild" offers a balanced view of what must be done to honor captive animals.
  • Around the world, about 700 million people visit a zoo or aquarium every year.
  • Despite good intentions, many zoo animals don't thrive and we’re still a long way off from much-needed reform.
A caged cheetah.
Source: Karen F/Pexels

The existence of zoos of all sorts in which a wide variety of animals are held captive raises countless ethical questions. Despite the best of intentions, most zoos do not overcome what are called "captivity effects" and existing laws do not protect their residents. For these and other reasons, I was pleased to learn of a new, well-researched book titled Born to Be Wild: Reckoning with the Zoo in the Age of Extinction, in which readers are taken behind the scenes of the most iconic zoos by award-winning writer Andrew Westoll, who shows that zoos often fail to protect the animals they work to save.

I found the book to be a valuable, balanced view of what really is happening on the ground at most zoos. It is not an anti-zoo rant but does ask a lot from them in the years to come.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Born to Be Wild?

Andrew Westoll: The central idea at the heart of the book is that no matter what you think about the zoo, we can all agree that absent a convincing argument to the contrary, every animal should be able to live the life it evolved to live.

One of my goals is to model how to explore a topic that challenges or confuses us with an open mind. Another is to help open a renewed dialogue about the position and power of a place that, aside from houses of worship, are the most influential public institutions in our society. Around the world, about 700 million people visit a zoo or aquarium every year. That’s about a tenth of humanity. Shouldn’t we all know a little more about how these places work?

Source: Rowman & Littlefield, used with permission

And finally, my other main goal is to take the reader to the heart of the modern zoo by taking them behind the scenes at some of the most interesting zoos on the planet. Readers get to go on every adventure I did, from the urban wilds of Central Park to the remote jungles of Central Africa.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

AW: Just to pick a few:

  1. Recent reporting suggests that giant panda breeding programs in China have very little to do with actual conservation efforts, and everything to do with exporting Chinese “soft power” (sorry for the pun) around the world. I visited the giant pandas of Vienna, at the Schönbrunn Zoo, to understand why the Austrians have had such success in breeding the bears naturally (i.e., without artificial insemination). It’s a remarkable story of persistence and expertise. But I also explored the fact that most countries to receive cute and cuddly diplomats from Beijing have first signed major trading deals with the Chinese state.

    Panda diplomacy is a troubling, exploitative practice in which the bears’ welfare is rarely the main priority. The next time we see a head of state posing with pandas at their local zoos, we should remember this fact.

  2. One of the most compelling arguments for the existence of the modern zoo is that the zoo is helping protect wild animals and wild places. But when you actually crunch the numbers, what you find is that a small handful of well-resourced, world-class zoos are doing the vast majority of the heavy lifting, and most zoos are just piggybacking on their accomplishments. When you remove the heavy hitters, it turns out that most zoos aren’t even giving 2% of their annual operating budgets to field conservation. Does that sound like an institution that has retooled for the Sixth Extinction, as zoo marketing departments would have us believe, or simply an institution that has figured out what sells in our climate-anxious culture?

  3. Breeding programs at zoo are enormously controversial, because no matter what a zoo tells us, animals born into zoos are destined to live their entire lives in a zoo. These breeding programs are supposed to be about building “assurance populations,” genetically robust populations that could one day be released back into the wild.

    However, when you look deeply at the breeding data, you discover that the majority of vertebrate populations being bred in zoos are not genetically viable (i.e., not genetically diverse enough to counteract the impacts of inbreeding). In other words, zoos around the world are failing at their most fundamental task: to build healthy, sustainable populations into the future.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

AW: Most books about the zoo are either scholarly or theoretical in nature, focused on specific histories or through the lens of animal rights. But most of them don’t do a great job of meeting regular people where they live. I want to engage everyday people in these ethical and moral questions, to help them think through their impressions of the modern zoo without feeling they’ve missed an entire semester of college!

MB: What has it been like to levy criticisms at the modern zoo as a whole, when so many people who work in them are well-intentioned and clearly care a great deal for their animals?

AW: This is probably the hardest part of my job as a journalist, to separate the people I’ve met and spoken with from the larger topics I’m dealing with. And this was especially hard in this case. Just about every zoo employee I interviewed or met while researching this book was a passionate animal person, wholly dedicated to the well-being of their charges, whether they were curators, keepers, or marketing folks.

But after reading so much of the zoo literature, where so many progressive people in the industry are begging their institutions to modernize and change for the better, and after learning just how deeply the zoo is failing to meet its own targets, it became clear to me that many zoo professionals have a permanent blind spot when it comes to considering the role of the modern zoo and the ethics of captivity in the 21st century.

It seems to me that if the zoo wants to maintain its social license to operate, it is going to have to radically update its thinking and its operational mandate. Zoo insiders have been calling for this to happen for more than 30 years now. Unfortunately, we’re still a long way off from the zoo renaissance we’ve been promised.

item.title: How to Inspire the Thanksgiving Spirit Year-Round
item.description:
Persuasion

How to Inspire the Thanksgiving Spirit Year-Round

When government agencies empower agency of the residents, people thrive.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Regardless of location or demographics, 72% of U.S. adults say the area where they live is worth investing in.
  • If they believe they will be heard, 2 out of 3 U.S. citizens are motivated to give back.
  • People assess personal life satisfaction based more on agency than on mood.
Community spirit improves well-being.
Source: Debbie Peterson

The tradition of Thanksgiving is an inspiring example of community and sharing that has strengthened North America for centuries. In February and March 2026, Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation asked 6,732 American citizens what motivates them to give to their communities. They wanted to know whether opportunity, another powerful American driving force, is still going strong. They asked whether people believe they can shape their own futures to build better lives and stronger communities, and how those views influence their willingness to give back.

They found that regardless of location or demographics, 72% of U.S. adults surveyed say the area where they live is worth investing in, even though nearly half do not agree that people in their community look out for one another or work together to solve common problems. Only 1 in 3 believe that if they had an idea to improve their community, someone would listen, and 60% do not trust their local leaders to act in the community's best interest. However, if they believe they will be heard, 2 out of 3 respondents are motivated to give back.

Factors That Influence Community Support and Well-Being

Beyond being listened to, citizens cited other factors that shape their love for and support of their communities. More than 8 in 10 say access to nature improves their quality of life. Americans living in places with closer interpersonal ties are more likely to feel like they can shape the direction of their lives. More than three-quarters believe housing is unaffordable, and nearly half say their communities do not offer enough stable jobs.

The researchers believe these responses reflect the psychological concept of agency, defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as the ability to take action or choose what action to take. They find that self-determination, or agency, is the most important predictor of adults’ assessment of their life satisfaction. Their data show that in communities that build strong foundations and connections among their residents, well-being and optimism flourish.

The foundation’s statistics are affirmed by the 2026 findings of Payne & Schimmack, professors at the University of Toronto's Psychological & Brain Sciences department. They also study the impact of opportunity, or agency, on individuals. They surveyed 1,200 adults from Canada and the United Kingdom to measure their positive and negative feelings, life satisfaction, and three psychological traits: autonomy—the feeling of being free to make choices; competence—feeling effective and capable; and relatedness—feeling close and connected to others.

Autonomy as a Predictor of Life Satisfaction

Their findings unwrap the statistics and responses reported by Gallup and Walton. They find that whether happy or sad, autonomy—the sense of freedom to make choices—is the strongest indicator of life satisfaction. "Those who felt more autonomous were more satisfied with their lives," said Payne, who said the findings have practical implications for public policy. "Programs and interventions designed to improve well-being may succeed in improving feelings, but if they restrict people's choices, then they could ultimately backfire and lead people to judge their lives as worse overall.”

The Walton Family Foundation sums it up: “Communities grow stronger when people have a voice and a way to contribute.” They find that those closest to challenges are also closest to local solutions for local problems if they are supported to speak up and contribute. “When we listen to the people who know their communities best, we can turn their ideas into lasting change.”

item.title: Do Your In-Laws Treat You Like Their Son’s Biggest Mistake?
item.description:
Relationships

Do Your In-Laws Treat You Like Their Son’s Biggest Mistake?

Why disrespecting you means disrespecting the family their son has built.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Maybe you married the love of your life, but that doesn't mean you'll win over the people who raised them.
  • Some in-laws seem to spend decades waiting for their child to finally come to their senses and get divorced.
  • Your in-laws don't have to love you, but they do have to respect the boundaries of the family you've built.
Source: Bear Photos/Shutterstock

Maybe you did marry the love of your life, but that still doesn't guarantee you'll win over the people who raised them. Some in-laws are loving and accept you with ease, while others seem to spend decades waiting for their son to finally come to his senses.

As a couples therapist, I've listened to stories of complicated in-law dynamics, ranging from mildly irritating to downright abusive, on a daily basis.

Maybe your career ambitions don't align with your in-laws' traditional expectations of what a wife and mother should be. You’re selfish for working or having a self-care routine, but if you stay home, you're accused of being lazy and mooching off their son.

Perhaps your mother-in-law was perfectly lovely for years, until your children reached adolescence, got their own phones, and your services in orchestrating family get-togethers were no longer needed. Suddenly, the woman who used to call you every week barely acknowledges your existence.

Maybe your sister-in-law crashed your family vacation, or your mother-in-law feels entitled to drop by your home whenever she pleases, and everyone expects you to go with the flow. Or your father-in-law has barely acknowledged you for a decade but couldn't contain his relief when your newborn baby looked exactly like his son and nothing like you.

You are bombarded with unsolicited advice about your finances, your diet, and your children's education.

Family relationships are complicated, and nobody should expect their in-laws to agree with or approve of every decision they make. However, repeatedly being made to feel unwelcome is not the same as a disagreement.

Your Marriage Is Your Family

Secure-functioning relationships are built on the couple bubble, a protective partnership in which emotional safety and connection for the couple are prioritized. This includes managing thirds, which can be anything the couple navigates, including relationships, careers, hobbies, obligations, and even addictions that can interfere with the stability of the partnership (Tatkin, 2024).

Managing extended-family dynamics doesn't mean cutting ties, although in some circumstances, distance may be necessary. Nor does it mean demanding that everyone accommodate you at all costs. But it does mean recognizing that as you build your life together with another person, you become one another’s primary attachment figure. Protecting the stability and safety of that relationship is a shared responsibility.

Both partners should be able to trust that they won't be abandoned when things get uncomfortable, especially when the discomfort comes from each other's family of origin.

Consider a husband whose mother repeatedly criticizes his wife, dismisses her parenting decisions, or excludes her from important family conversations. The husband may feel that because his mother treats him warmly, the problem is between the two women. He may even insist that his wife is being too sensitive and expect her to let it go in order to keep the peace. This is exactly how the couple bubble begins to break down.

Being Nice When Things Are Good Isn’t Enough

One of the more challenging dynamics in extended families is the relationship that seems perfectly pleasant until someone sets a boundary.

Your in-laws may be affectionate, attentive, and generous when you are agreeable, show up every Sunday for dinner, accept their unsolicited advice, and remain available whenever they need something. But the moment you decide to spend the holidays elsewhere or decline a financial request, the warmth disappears.

In healthy families, people are not loving only when they are being accommodated and unpleasant the minute someone exercises their autonomy. Boundaries around your home, time, money, and decisions that affect your immediate family are part of being an independent adult and building a life with your partner. Your in-laws might not agree with or love these boundaries, but they do have to respect them.

Children Are Watching How Their Parents Are Treated

Children depend on their parents and caregivers to provide them with a safe container where they can play and grow. Their early attachment figures help them determine whether people are safe and predictable, whether conflict can be managed, and whether the people they depend on have the capacity to protect them.

Imagine a child at a family gathering where one parent is repeatedly interrupted, criticized, or excluded from the conversation. Perhaps their parenting decisions are openly questioned, or they are surrounded by relatives who make jokes at their expense while everyone else laughs. The child may not understand the content of the disagreement, but they can sense the tension.

When a parent is undermined, ignored, or humiliated in front of them and other family members, children may feel unsafe and receive damaging messages about loyalty and commitment.

This doesn't mean children need to see their parents as invulnerable or that witnessing an occasional disagreement will be irreparable. In fact, seeing adults navigate conflict respectfully and repair ruptures is an important part of development. However, repeatedly watching a parent be treated as though their feelings, authority, or presence don't matter disrupts the child’s sense of safety and trust.

Protecting children doesn't require pretending that everyone gets along. It does, however, require showing them that the adults responsible for their well-being can stand up for themselves and one another.

Your In-Laws Don’t Have to Love You

In couples therapy, one of the recurring challenges I see is the tension between loyalty to one's family of origin and loyalty to the partnership.

For some people, setting boundaries with parents can evoke a tremendous amount of shame and guilt. They may have grown up believing that keeping their parents happy was how they would be lovable, that disagreements were unacceptable, and that love meant accommodating everyone else's needs. As adults, they may continue to prioritize avoiding parental disappointment, even when doing so comes at the expense of their own family they're trying to build.

The partner who grew up in a family that is the source of conflict may have learned to tolerate behaviors that feel unacceptable, intrusive, or outright hostile to the other partner.

Damage to the couplehood is more preventable when the partner whose family is involved assumes responsibility for communicating boundaries.

The goal isn't to force everyone to like each other or to turn every insensitive comment into a family dispute. Healthy relationships don’t require everyone to be best friends, but they do require mutual respect.

Your in-laws don't have to think you're the greatest thing that ever happened to their family, but they do have to recognize that disrespecting you means disrespecting the family he's chosen to build.
